conversation.content:
Good morning, Sarah. I’m so glad you were able to come in today. My name is Maya—I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician here at the clinic, and I spend my days helping new mothers sort through all the feelings that can show up after a baby arrives.

Today we’re going to use a short, well-trusted questionnaire called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—usually just called the **EPDS**. It’s a simple 10-question check-in that helps us see how you’ve been coping emotionally over the past seven days. There’s no pass-or-fail; it’s just a way for us to make sure we’re giving you the right support.

Everything we talk about stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger, so please answer as honestly as you can. We’ll move through the questions at whatever pace feels comfortable, and if anything feels hard to say out loud, we can pause and talk it through. Ready to begin?

Let’s start with the first question:

In the past week, when you think about moments you were able to laugh or see the funny side of things, how often did that happen for you?

[Offers a small, tired smile.]  
Honestly…? I can still laugh, but it feels kind of forced. I’d say maybe half the time something funny comes up, I’ll chuckle, but it doesn’t feel as light or natural as it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[slow nod, eyes on the floor]  
Mostly yes…but it’s like the laugh dies off quicker. I’ll smile at something silly my husband says or a goofy face the baby makes, yet the next second I’m just… flat again. I still laugh, just not with that easy feeling I remember.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs a little, voice quiet]

I try to look forward to stuff—like taking the baby for walks or having my mom over—but the excitement feels kind of… dimmed. I still plan things and want them to be nice, yet when the moment comes it’s more “going through the motions” than actually enjoying it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes flick down to my lap, shoulders hunch]

Sometimes... like last night when she wouldn't settle for two hours, I kept thinking maybe I ate something that bothered her, or I didn't swaddle her tight enough. My head knows babies just cry, but a little voice still says, "You messed up." It doesn't happen every time, but when I'm extra tired, the blame sneaks in.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[twists the edge of my sweater]

Yeah... most evenings my chest feels tight for no real reason. I'll check if she's breathing every few minutes, even though the monitor's on. Nothing specific triggered it—I just get this knot that something might go wrong, and I can't shake it off for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[wrings hands]

A couple of times this week—like when I was grocery shopping—my heart suddenly raced and I felt shaky, like I had to get out of there. I wasn’t worried about anything I could name; it just hit and then passed after a few minutes. It’s not every day, but it’s unsettling when it happens.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales slowly]

Yes... most days feel like I'm juggling while running on empty. One second I'm feeding her, next it's laundry, texts I forgot to answer, dishes piling up—and suddenly I'm near tears because I can't find a clean burp cloth. I keep telling myself it's normal new-mom chaos, but it still feels overwhelming more often than not.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quietly]  
A few nights this week I lay there staring at the ceiling long after the baby settled. My mind just loops—worrying I’m doing everything wrong, replaying every little cry—and I can’t drift off. I wouldn’t say I’m “so unhappy,” but the sadness and tension keep me awake for an hour or more.
I have felt sad or miserable

[swallows hard, eyes water a bit]

Yeah... I get waves of sadness most days. It’s not constant, but out of nowhere I’ll feel this heavy, empty pit in my chest—like I miss something I can’t name. I’ll cry for a minute, wipe my face, and go back to whatever I was doing. It lifts after a while, but it keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[Voice drops to a whisper, eyes fixed on my lap]

Only once this week... yesterday afternoon. She finally napped, the house was quiet, and I just sat on the couch feeling this heavy ache. Tears came for a couple minutes—nothing set it off, just this wave of "I can’t do all this." Then I wiped my face and kept going.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No—I haven’t had any thoughts like that. When things feel overwhelming I just want help, not to hurt myself.

Sarah, it sounds as though you're working tirelessly to care for your daughter while carrying a steady weight of sadness, worry and self-doubt. You described laughter that quickly fades, plans that feel flat, evenings of tight-chested anxiety, and sudden waves of tears. These feelings are understandably frightening and exhausting, yet they do not diminish the love and effort you pour into motherhood every day.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 17, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient still makes plans but reports enjoyment is "dimmed" and feels like "going through the motions," matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent self-blame that surfaces under stress but not in every situation, aligning with "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, persistent, unexplained anxiety with physical symptoms and intrusive worries, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, unexplained panic episodes occurring multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent daily overwhelm and tearfulness yet still functioning, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent sleep difficulty due to persistent worry and sadness, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent waves of sadness "most days", consistent with "quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** With a score of 17 (>13) Sarah meets screening criteria for probable major <med>postpartum depression</med> with co-occurring <med>anxiety</med>. She endorses diminished interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), most-days sadness, unwarranted guilt, recurrent worry, two panic attacks this week, and sleep disruption unrelated to infant needs. Symptom onset within four weeks postpartum aligns with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with her <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to confirm diagnosis and discuss treatment options
2. Offer immediate referral to a perinatal <med>mental health specialist</med> for evidence-based therapy such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med>
3. Discuss safety plan and 24-hour family support until professional review
4. Encourage 20-30 minutes of outdoor daylight walking with baby to help regulate mood and sleep
5. Provide contact details for local <med>postpartum support groups</med> and national helplines for ongoing reassurance
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 17: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Source: self-report + behavioral observation (10-item EPDS-style questions)

Symptoms / concerns endorsed  
– Anhedonia: diminished capacity for sustained pleasure (“laugh dies off,” “excitement dimmed”)  
– Recurrent low mood/sadness with tearfulness, occurring most days  
– Unwarranted self-blame regarding infant care  
– Persistent, generalized anxiety with physical symptoms (tight chest)  
– Two recent panic-like episodes (grocery, sudden racing heart)  
– Subjective sense of being overwhelmed, “running on empty”  
– Initial insomnia linked to ruminative worry/sadness, several nights/week  
– Crying spell without clear precipitant  

Positive findings relevant to postpartum mood disorders  
1. Meets screening threshold for probable depression (≥6/10 items endorsed with clinical features)  
2. Meets screening threshold for co-occurring anxiety symptoms (GAD-7 style items positive)  
3. Onset within context of recent childbirth (typical for PPD/PPA)  

Risk factors identified  
– Daily low mood, anhedonia, tearfulness  
– Sleep disruption secondary to mood (not solely infant care demands)  
– Excessive guilt/self-criticism  
– Anxiety attacks & chronic worry  
– Impaired coping (“near tears,” avoidance of stores)  

Safety concern  
– Denies any thoughts of self-harm (Q10 negative)  
– No suicidal ideation elicited at this screening  

Summary  
Patient exhibits multiple depressive and anxious symptoms of moderate intensity emerging postpartum, with functional impact on enjoyment, sleep, and day-to-day coping. No current self-harm ideation. Recommend further assessment with standardized EPDS and clinical interview to confirm provisional diagnosis and determine appropriate level of care.
